transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-13 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Romero (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Tom Keller (CTO - Sundial), Maya Chen (Eng Mgr), Jared Li (SRE), Lina Park (Product)

Auto Summary: quick intake on reserved capacity, wanting isolation for PII workloads, burst to hosted API during traffic spikes, interest in VPC/private and hybrid on-prem later.

Topics: reserved GPU sizing, hot pool pre-warm, eviction and failover, KMS + audit logs, SSO, model pinning and rollout policies.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh two quick intros, I'm Alex, AE on the infra team and Priya's our solutions engineer, we'll run through your capacity needs and then dive into the technicals.
[00:18] Tom (Sundial): Hey, Tom here. Quick context: we're building a real-time summarization feature for financial docs, so PII is a concern, latency target is sub-200ms p95 for short prompts, and we expect big spikes around earnings days.
[00:34] Priya (Redwood SE): Great, thanks Tom. Can you give us ballpark QPS and token sizes during baseline vs spike? that helps us size reserved pools vs burst.
[00:48] Maya (Sundial): Baseline around 40 qps, spikes up to 900 qps for short windows (5-20 minutes) during events, avg payload ~120 tokens, heavy tail to 800 tokens for deep summaries.
[01:05] Jared (SRE): Also want to note compliance: all PII must be encrypted at rest, audit logs retained for 2 years and we use our KMS for key management if possible.
[01:18] Alex: Got it. So two parts here: steady reserved capacity to hit low latency, and a burst plan that either pre-warms extra nodes or fails over to Redwood hosted endpoints during bursts. We call the dedicated offering "Reserved GPU" which gives you predictable throughput and isolation.
[01:36] Tom: On isolation — do you support tenant fencing so other customers can't noisy-neighbor our models? we need hard isolation for some tenants with sensitive data.
[01:48] Priya: Yes, we support dedicated pools with tenant fencing and strict tenancy. There are two flavors: per-tenant reserved pools, or shared reserved pools with stricter cgroups and isolation controls. We also have warm pools (hot-pools) to pre-warm models.
[02:05] Maya: What's the eviction behavior when you pre-warm? we can't have active requests get dropped during scale-up.
[02:12] Priya: Good question. Our runtime uses graceful preemption — in practice we try to route new requests to warmed capacity and keep existing KV-caches alive where possible. Sometimes the transcription misses KV cache and writes K V cash which is funny. But effectively the cold-start path is minimized.
[02:35] Tom: If we go hybrid, how does data flow work if we failover to hosted? do we need to scrub PII first?
[02:44] Alex: For regulatory tenants you can mark routes as "no-remote" so they never go to hosted. For other routes you can set fallback policies: e.g., overflow to hosted only for non-PII endpoints. We can also support tokenization/PII redaction proxies on your side.
[02:59] Jared: About KMS — can Redwood integrate with our cloud KMS and HSMs? we want customer-managed keys.
[03:10] Priya: Yes, Redwood Private supports BYOK integrations with cloud KMS and on-prem HSMs. Audit logs are available via the console and can be exported into your SIEM.
[03:22] Lina (Product): Timeline question — if we commit to a 12-month reserved pool, what lead time for capacity provisioning?
[03:31] Alex: Typical lead time for dedicated GPUs is 4-8 weeks depending on region and SKU. For urgent cases we have burst credits and warm-pool options to bridge the gap.
[03:40] Tom: Cost tradeoffs — how do we think about p99 latency vs cost with batching and quantization?
[03:49] Priya: There's a clear tradeoff: heavier batching reduces unit cost but can increase tail latency. For low-latency workflows we recommend single-token streaming and smaller batch sizes, plus quantized model variants for cost efficiency. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles based on your workload.
[04:10] Maya: We run two model variants today — a base 13B for most workloads and a 70B for higher-quality summaries. Can Redwood serve model variants and fallback automatically?
[04:21] Priya: Yes, you can pin outputs to model versions and set rollout/fallback policies. During capacity constraints the router can fall back to cheaper variants, or route to hosted variants.
[04:34] Tom: On benchmarks — we want p50/p95/p99 across baseline and spike, and cost per 1k tokens for each variant.
[04:41] Alex: We'll include that in the benchmark plan. Priya will run an initial synthetic test, then we'd like to run a test with your real payloads if you can provide them.
[04:53] Jared: About network — we need VPC peering or PrivateLink to avoid public endpoints.
[05:00] Priya: Both are supported. For Redwood Private you can deploy in your VPC; for Dedicated we support VPC peering and PrivateLink depending on region. We'll note the exact network topology in the security brief.
[05:14] Tom: Are there any known issues with long-context models and KV cache persistence in multi-tenant settings?
[05:24] Priya: We manage KV cache per worker, and the runtime keeps it pinned where possible. In worst-case eviction we try to warm a copy from prefix cache. There are edge cases for very long-context 70B sequences where memory pressure causes more frequent evictions — that'll factor into sizing.
[05:44] Maya: For burst strategy, are customers typically comfortable failing over to the hosted API? our security team is cautious.
[05:53] Alex: Many customers split routes: PII routes stay on private/dedicated, public or anonymized routes have fallback to hosted. Also we can set rate-limits and surge window policies to avoid wholesale failover.
[06:07] Lina: Any compliance certifications we should be aware of?
[06:12] Priya: Redwood holds SOC2 Type II and we're working on ISO 27001. We can share the compliance pack and a whitepaper on PII handling.
[06:21] Tom: Competitors — we've evaluated Vertex and a couple of open-source runtimes; they either lacked the ops controls or were too expensive at scale.
[06:32] Alex: Noted. For commercial terms we typically have monthly usage for Hosted, reserved monthly commits for Dedicated, and enterprise licensing for Private. We'll send a tiered pricing sheet.
[06:44] Maya: One more technical — autoscaling behavior under sustained 30-minute bursts, will you autoscale or do we need to pre-provision?
[06:54] Priya: Autoscaling is configurable: you can set cooldowns and max scaling limits. For short spikes (under 30 mins) hot-pools + pre-warm is recommended; for sustained months-long increases we recommend resizing commitments.
[07:08] Tom: Ok, sounds good. Let's talk through the specific numbers: baseline 40 qps, spike 900 qps, average 120 tokens. Any quick back-of-envelope sizing?
[07:18] Priya: Roughly, a 40 qps baseline with your 13B model can be served with a small reserved pool (2-3 GPUs depending on GPU type). To absorb 900 qps spikes you'd need either a large warm pool or burst to hosted; fully reserved at that scale is expensive. We'll model three scenarios in the pricing doc.
[07:38] Alex: Action items recap: Alex send pricing; Priya prepare benchmark plan; Jared share traffic. We'll schedule the 2-hour benchmark session after Jared shares the payloads.
[07:50] Tom: Thanks all. One last ask — include an ops runbook for incident playbooks (what happens if a warm-pool fails).
[07:58] Priya: We'll include a runbook snippet in the benchmark package.

End notes: call ended ~52 minutes after deep Q/A and negotiation on timelines.

Questions (recorded):
- "Can Redwood do customer-managed KMS?" Answer: yes, BYOK supported for Private and Dedicated (subject to contract)
- "Can we failover to hosted for non-PII only?" Answer: yes via route-level policies

Links referenced: Pricing playbook (link to sent later), SOC2 package (link to share), benchmark plan doc (to be created).
